titleStmt.title: Determining Actual Response Time in P-FRP using Idle-Period Game Board *

analytic.title: Determining Actual Response Time in P-FRP using Idle-Period Game Board *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A * new, purely functional model of computation, called Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP), has been introduced as a new paradigm for building real-time software. P-FRP allows assignment of static priorities to tasks and guarantees that, when a higher priority task is released, the system will immediately preempt any lowerpriority tasks that may be executing at the time. This execution model is different from the classical preemptive model † of realtime systems due to the abort nature of preempted tasks. Methods developed for determining actual response time in the preemptive model are not guaranteed to work in P-FRP. In previous work, the gap-enumeration technique has been presented as a viable alternative to simulations for computing actual response time in P-FRP. Unfortunately, this method is difficult to implement due to its use of a Red-Black tree which is not available as a native function in programming languages. Also this method requires a complex logic loop for finding idle periods. In this paper, we present another technique using game-board which is simple to implement and uses native data structures. However, this simplicity comes at a performance cost which has also been analyzed in this paper.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Functional programming paradigm is based on the mathematical principles of lamda (λ)-calculus. A formal definition of functional programming was given by Backus [3], who introduced the FP programming language. Since then, many flavors of Function programming languages have been developed including OCaml, Haskell and Scheme. Functional languages are also called declarative languages as they are mainly concerned with computational logic rather than control flow.

Using functional programming languages over the traditional imperative programming style found in C/C++, Java, Ada etc. offers several advantages, especially for implementing safety-critical systems. In this programming paradigm, the programmer can intuitively describe safety behaviors of the system, lowering the chance of introducing bugs in the design phase, while its stateless nature of execution does not require use of synchronization primitives, reducing the complexity of programming. Functional Reactive Programming has been implemented for applications like robotics [16], embedded controllers [12] and computer animation [17]. FRP [21] was developed as a domain specific language in Haskell. A subset of FRP was used to develop RT-FRP [19], where the space and time cost of execution is bounded, making it ideal for resource constrained embedded systems. A compilation strategy is proposed to convert a modified RT-FRP language into efficient imperative code [20]. The language of this new system called E-FRP is for use in embedded real-time controllers, and has been tested on a small microcontroller driven robot. The event execution in E-FRP follows the simple first-in-first-out order which may cause some events to miss their deadline leading to potentially catastrophic results in real-time systems.

To overcome this, a priority based E-FRP system, called priority-based FRP (P-FRP) [13] has been developed. P-FRP retains the exact computational semantics of E-FRP, but uses fixed priority scheduling to pre-assign a priority number to every event before execution. Hence, P-FRP offers guarantees for both responsiveness and resource boundness, making it ideal for memory and power constrained systems. However, a requirement in the functional programming model is that the state of the system cannot be changed, and no function can have side effects. To maintain this guarantee of stateless execution, the functional programming paradigm requires the execution of a function to be atomic in nature. To comply with this requirement, as well as allow preemption of lower priority events, P-FRP implements a transactional model of execution. Using only a copy of the state during event processing, and atomically committing these changes at the end of the event handler ( or task), a multi-version commit model of execution is implemented. This ensures that handling an event is an "all or nothing" proposition, and ensures the atomicity of handling an event.

This transactional execution model used in P-FRP is not new, and several such models have been presented in the past. These are the transactional memory systems [11], lockfree execution for critical sections [1] and preemptable atomic regions in Java [15]. The development of these systems was primarily motivated by the need to avoid concurrency related issues. Studies on the temporal properties of the transactional model are being done by some research groups. However, the response time studies currently available [1], [10], [15] provide basic schedulability analysis using approximate values or bounds on response times. Though approximate values or bounds only provide a general idea on the schedulability of tasks, the methods to compute them are much faster [6], [8], [18].

In this paper, we use the term 'actual' to differentiate from approximate or bounded response time. Actual response time is a more accurate indicator of temporal properties and is required in the design phase of a real-time system, or in developing exact schedulability tests. A study to find actual response time in transactional memory or lock-free execution has not been presented yet. An iterative method first presented by Audsley et al [2] (termed Audsley's method in this paper), is a common approach for determining actual response time in the preemptive model. However, this method is not guaranteed to work with P-FRP (see section 3 for example).

In [13], [18], basic results on schedulability and approximate upper bounds on response times of P-FRP tasks have been presented. In [4], [5], we have addressed the problem of determining actual response time in P-FRP. One straightforward way, is to use a time-accurate simulation (TAS) that progresses through every time tick, and runs tasks based on the P-FRP execution model. Another method in [4], [5] is the gap-enumeration method which enumerates all idle periods in a tree like structure. Though the gapenumeration method offers significant performance enhancements over time-accurate simulation, implementing it is not easy due to the presence of a tree and complex logic to determine idle periods. Using the same principle as the gap-enumeration method, we present a new technique using a game-board that can determine exact response time of P-FRP tasks. This technique is simple to implement and offers significant performance enhancements over time-accurate simulation. However, relative to gap-enumeration it has some performance degradation.

div.head: A. Contributions
div.p: This paper presents a new algorithm to determine the actual response time of tasks in P-FRP. It offers performance improvements over a simulation based approach, and simplicity of implementation relative to the previously developed gap-enumeration method. We first look at a common method to determine actual response time in the preemptive model (Section 3) as well as its extension for P-FRP (section 3.1), that does not work for several cases. A technique to determine actual response time using idle-periods (section 4) is presented, along with the fixed size game-board method to implement this technique (section 5). We then improve upon this technique to use dynamic size game boards (section 5.1). Performance comparisons of fixed and dynamic size game board relative to time-accurate simulation and the gap-enumerations methods using task sets of different sizes are provided (Section 6).

The paper concludes with a review of related work (Section 7) and a reflection on our results (Section 8).The utility of this work presented in this paper also extends to determining actual response time in systems which have similar execution models, like in transactional memory [11] and atomic critical sections of Java [15].

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS AND EXECUTION MODEL OF P-FRP
div.p: In this section, we introduce the basic concepts and the notation used to denote these concepts in the rest of the paper. In addition, we review the P-FRP execution model and assumptions made in this study.

div.head: A. Basic Concepts
div.p: Essential concepts for P-FRP are tasks and their associated priority, their associated time period and the dual concept of arrival rate, and their processing time; the concept of a time interval and release offset therein. In our task model, all these assumed to be known a priori. The notation and formal definitions for these concepts as well as a few others used in the paper are as follows:

• Let task set Γ n = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,…, τ n } be a set of n periodic tasks • The priority of τ k ∈ Γ n is the positive integer k, where a higher number implies higher priority. Associating higher values with higher priority is a standard in Linux and Windows operating systems • T k is the arrival time period between two successive jobs of τ k • C k is the worst-case execution time for τ k • t copy (k) is the time taken to make a copy of the state before τ k starts execution (see section 2.2.1) • t restore (k) is the time taken to restore the state after τ k has completed execution (see section 2.2.1) • P k is the processing time for τ k . Processing of a task includes execution as well as copy and restore operations. Hence, P k = t copy (k) + C k + t restore (k) • R k,m represents the release time of the m th job of τ k • Φ k represents the release offset which is the release time of the first job of τ k . Or,

div.head: B. Execution Model and Assumptions
div.p: In this study, all tasks are assumed to execute in a uniprocessor system with no precedence constraints. When job of a higher priority task τ i is released, it can immediately preempt an executing lower priority task, and changes made by the lower priority task are rolled back. The lower priority task will be restarted when the higher priority task has completed processing. Due to P-FRP's transactional nature of execution, all tasks are assumed to run without concurrency constraints. To derive the actual response time of a task τ j , we have considered the release offset of τ j to be 0.

When some task is released, it enters a processing queue Q which is arranged by priority order, such that all arriving higher priority tasks are moved to the head of the queue. The length of the queue is bounded, and no two instances of the same task can be present in the queue at the same time. This requires a task to complete processing before the release of its next job. To maintain this requirement, we assume a hard real-time system with task deadline equal to the time period between jobs. A task set is schedulable in some time interval only if no task in the set has a deadline miss.

Once τ i enters Q two situations are possible. If a task of lower priority than i is being processed, it will be immediately preempted and τ i will start processing. If a task of higher priority than τ i is being processed, then τ i will wait in the Q and start processing only after the higher priority task has completed. An exception to the immediate preemption is made during copy and restore operations which is explained in the following paragraph.

div.head: C. Copy and Restore Operations
div.p: In P-FRP, when a task starts processing it creates a 'scratch' state, which is a copy of the current state of the system. Changes made during the processing of this task are maintained inside such a state. When the task has completed, the 'scratch' state is restored into the final state in an atomic operation. Therefore, during the restoration and copy operations, the task being processed cannot be preempted by higher priority tasks. If the task is preempted after copy but before the restore operation, the scratch state is simply discarded. The context-switch between tasks only involves a state copy operation for the task that will be commencing processing. The time taken for copy (t copy (k)) and restore (t restore (k)) operations of τ k is part of the processing time of the task, P k .

For the methods presented in this paper, the values of t copy (k) and t restore (k) for all tasks are kept same and equal to a single discrete time unit of processing. Hence, ∀k∈Γ n , t copy (k)= t restore (k) =1.

These values of t copy (k) and t restore (k) are reasonable, as copy and restore operations are only a fraction of the worst-case execution time of the task. However, our method can be extended to consider situations where the values of t restore (k) and t copy (k) are variable, and we will focus on these cases in a separate short paper.

div.head: D. Critical Instant in P-FRP
div.p: In response time analysis for fixed-priority scheduling, a critical-instant of release is assumed. Critical instant is the time, at which task releases lead to the worst-case response time (WCRT) [14] of the task being analyzed. In their seminal work, Liu and Layland [14] showed that in fixed-priority scheduling for the preemptive model, the critical-instant for a lower priority task τ i occurs when it is released at the same time as all higher priority tasks. Or, the release offset of task τ j and higher priority tasks is the same (synchronous release) As shown in [4], for P-FRP, a synchronous release of τ i and higher priority tasks is not guaranteed to result in the WCRT of τ i .

The method presented in this paper, determines the response time of a task only for a user specified release offset of higher priority tasks. Hence, the release offsets required by the methods presented in this paper, are assumed to be know a priori. These release offsets, may or may not lead to the WCRT for the task being analyzed. To determine the WCRT for a given P-FRP task, all possible combinations of release offsets of higher priority tasks have to be generated. Then the response time under each release scenario has to be computed using the method presented in this paper. The maximum value of computed response times, will be the WCRT of the task. For this reason, an efficient method for determining response time under a given release scenario is all the more important in P-FRP.

Clearly, Audsley's method, and its modified version are not guaranteed to compute the actual response time in P-FRP. Another way to determining such response time is the Time Accurate-Simulation (TAS), algorithm for which is given in [4]. TAS executes a loop that goes through every time tick and simulates the execution of task based on the P-FRP execution model. TAS requires separate data structures for maintaining a task queue as well as for keeping track of executing tasks. In [4], it was shown that the number of steps executed by TAS is proportional to the response time of the task, and TAS performed closest to the gapenumeration method for tasks with lower response times. Since it executes for every discrete time, it is inefficient in several practical cases where processing time for tasks can run into several thousands of milliseconds.

div.head: IV. DETERMINING RESPONSE TIME USING IDLE PERIODS
div.p: In this section, we show how the response time of a lower priority task can be determined by analyzing idleperiods of tasks. Before that we introduce a property that relates idle periods with the schedulability of tasks in P-FRP. τ2 and τ3 respectively. The 'Abort' tag shows the time when τ1 or τ2 are aborted by higher priority tasks Property 1: For task τ j to be schedulable, one level-(j+1) idle period of at least length P j will exist between every two successive jobs of τ j . Proof. To complete processing, τ j should be processed for P j time, without any interference from higher priority tasks. Since no task having a higher priority than j is available to be processed in a level-(j+1) idle period, τ j will require at least one level-(j+1) idle period of minimum size P j to complete processing. This level-(j+1) idle period should be available before the arrival of its new job, otherwise τ j will have a deadline miss.

Let us now see the mechanism of determining exact response time using idle periods. For task set Γ n = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,…,τ n }, we have to determine the response time of the first job of τ j (RT j ) (j < n). Assume all tasks are released at the same time as τ j (time 0). We know that τ j can only be processed in level-(j+1) idle periods. These level-(j+1) idle periods are created after the processing of tasks τ n to τ j+1 . From property 1, we know that one level-(j+1) idle period in the time interval [0, T j ) has to be larger than P j , for τ j to be schedulable. We will first find all the level-(j+1) idle periods in the period [0,T j ) and then search through these for a level-(j+1) idle period larger than P j . τ j will be processed in this level-(j+1) idle period making the response time of τ j equal to t 1 + P j , where t 1 is the start time of idle period.

To find the level-(j+1) idle periods in which τ j can be processed, we progressively analyze idle periods left by the processing of all higher priority tasks. The level-(n+1)idle period that is available for τ n to run, is the entire length of the time interval [0, T j ). The first job of τ n will be released at time 0, and the second at time T n . The m th job of τ n will be released at (m-1)•T n . The level-n idle period created between the 1 st and 2 nd job is [P n , T n ). Similarly the level-n idle period created between the 2 nd and 3 rd job is [T n +P n , 2•T n ). Once all jobs of τ n have been accounted for in the interval [0, T j ), jobs of τ n-1 are processed in the available level-n idle periods. After all jobs of τ n-1 have completed processing in the interval [0, T j ), level-(n-1) idle periods are created, in which jobs of τ n-2 will be processed. This way all the remaining tasks are consecutively processed, and after accounting for the processing of tasks till τ j+1 , level-(j+1) idle periods are formed. A search is done on these level-(j+1) idle periods to determine the first such period who's size is more than or equal to P j and the response time of τ j (RT j ) will be :
RT j = t + P j , where t is the start time of this level-(j+1) idle period.

div.head: V. GAME BOARD FOR DETERMINING RESPONSE TIME
div.p: The mechanism of determining actual response time for task τ j , presented in section 4 can be implemented by using a linear game board of size T j . Each block in the game board represents a unit of time, and block can either be marked or unmarked. We start from the highest priority task τ n , and mark the blocks based on the processing of all jobs of τ n in the interval [0, T j ). We then fill the block jobs based on jobs of τ n-1 in the interval [0, T j ). This way the game board is filled till all jobs of τ n-j have been accounted for. Then we can do a search on the board to look for the first consecutive unfilled blocks of size P j , to determine the response time of τ j .
For the m th job of task τ i , the game-board is marked based on the following simple rules. The variable mark represents the number of blocks that have been marked by this job:

• Start from block number Φ i + (m-1)•T i • If the block in unmarked, mark it with task identifier and increment mark by 1, proceed to next block • If a block is marked with a different task identifier, reset mark to 0 and proceed to next block • If mark = P i , the m th job of τ i has completed processing

The game board for the example considered in the previous section is shown in Figures 3(a), 3(b) and 3(c). Figure 3(c) shows the state of the game board after tasks 3 and 2 have completed processing, leaving level-2 idle periods for τ 1 to complete processing in. Programmatically, a game board can be easily implemented using a fixed size single dimension array.

div.head: A. Dynamic Game-Board
div.p: So far, we have seen how a linear game board having T j blocks can be used to determine the actual response time of tasks τ 1 and τ 2 . However, evaluating all the level-(j+1) idle periods in the time interval [0,T j ), is required only when the exact response time of τ j will be close to its deadline. In several cases the response time of τ j will be much before T j , and a larger number of gaps than required, will be analyzed.

It is possible to start with a game board of a small size, and increase the size in fixed increments if the response time of τ j is not found. A question that arises, is the initial size of the game-board and the size of the increments. At a minimum, we will have to analyze the level-(j+1) idle periods left between at least two consecutive jobs of every task having higher priority than τ j . Let, P max represent the highest value of arrival period among all tasks having higher priority than τ j , Or,

div.p: Let τ max represent the higher priority task with arrival period of P max , and let Φ max be its release offset. Hence, if we analyze all level-(j+1) idle periods in the time interval [0, Φ max + P max ), at least two jobs of all tasks having a higher priority than j will be released. We can also increment the time interval by P max allowing us to look for level-(j+1) idle periods in which at least two jobs of every higher priority task have been released. Hence, in this paper, we set the initial size of the interval to [0, Φ max + P max ) and increment it by P max , till a level-(j+1) idle period in which τ j can complete processing is found.

A similar dynamic interval technique was presented for the gap-enumeration technique [4]. In this technique, gaps were first enumerated in the interval [0,   m T j / ), and the interval is incremented by the   m T j / in each subsequent iteration. m is an integer constant specified by the user. Since, the idle periods were stored in a tree data structure, the tree had to be rebuilt every time the time interval was incremented. In the game board, the level-(j+1) idle periods do not have to be re-analyzed from the beginning. Ideally, we should analyze the level-(j+1) idle periods only in the incremented time interval. Or, if we start by analyzing the periods in the time interval [0, Φ max + P max ), in the following iterations we should only analyze the level-(j+1) idle periods that come in time intervals [Φ max + P max , Φ max +2•P max ), [ Φ max + 2•P max , Φ max +3•P max ), and so on. For the p th (p > 0) iteration we analyze the level-(j+1) idle periods in the interval [Φ max + (p-1)•P max , Φ max + p•P max ).

However, some tasks that did not complete processing in [Φ max + p•P max , Φ max + (p+1)•P max ) will have to be accounted for in the next interval [Φ max + (p+1)•P max , Φ max + (p+2)•P max ). div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION
div.p: We have randomly generated 3 groups (groups A, B and C) of 500 schedulable task sets. Task sets in group A have 3 tasks, group B, 5 tasks and group C, 7 tasks. Each of the task sets in each group is unique in the sense, that at least 1 task is different between any two task sets. The arrival period for each of the tasks in all the 3 groups were selected from the range [40,60], while the processing times were selected from [4,10]. All tasks were assumed to be released simultaneously and the response time of the lowest priority task (τ 1 ) in each group was determined using the game-board (GB), gap-enumeration (GE) , and the Time-Accurate Simulations (TAS) algorithms. We used computational steps, which is the number of times major iterations inside an algorithm are executed, as a performance metric for the TAS, GB and GE algorithms. Since none of the % values exceed 100, it is clear that GB performs much better than TAS and the number of com-putational steps is in the 20% -70% range relative to TAS. The relative performance seems to improve with larger task sets. This is because with greater number of tasks, the response time of τ 1 will generally be higher, hence TAS will take more time. It is also clear that the dynamic game-board size algorithm performs better than fixed size game-board.

The results also show that even though both the game board and gap-enumeration methods perform better than a simulation, using GB leads to lower performance relative to the GE algorithm. Only in task sets with 7 tasks, is the performance of GB and GE similar for several task sets. The performance degradation in GB is attributed to the high search cost of search for level-2 idle periods in the gameboard. In the GE algorithm, the level-2 idle periods are stored in a efficient tree based data structure with a logarithmic search time. Also, the GE algorithm focuses only on idle periods using a complex gap-transformation function. In GB, every job of a task is executed for discrete time like in TAS, but unlike TAS, GB does not iterate over time intervals where no tasks are executing.

However, the performance difference between GE and GB is not severe, and because of its easy implementation we use the game board method extensively in our research on modeling temporal properties of P-FRP.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: Audsley et al [2] have presented an iterative method to compute actual response time in the preemptive model. Kaibachev et al [13] present a basic response time analysis for P-FRP by placing restrictions on execution times of higher priority tasks. The authors have derived the response time bound of a task as equal to its arrival period. Ras and Cheng [18], have presented response time analysis and have compared the performance of P-FRP execution with priority inversion strategies. The authors present a method to derive upper bound on response time by extending the iterative method developed by Audsley et al [2]. However, as shown in this paper, this method is unusable for most task sets. Both [13], [18] do not define any method to compute actual response times for P-FRP.

Transactional memory systems have been described by Herlihy and Moss [11]. Response time analysis for transaction memory using dynamic scheduling for multiprocessor systems has been done by Fahmy et al [10]. In Manson et al [15] atomic processing of the critical sections has been im- plemented in Java. Davis and Burns [8] derive upper bounds on response time for fixed priority scheduling building upon the work done by Bini and Baruah [6]. Anderson et al [1] do response time analysis of the lock-free mechanism. Lockfree is a mechanism to avoid priority inversion, the implementation of which is via an unconditional loop that terminates when the necessary updates to the shared resource are complete. Comparisons between transaction memory based systems and lock-free processing and benefits of the former have been shown in Herlihy and Moss [11].

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: A common method for determining actual response time in the preemptive model cannot be applied to P-FRP, due to the abort of preempted tasks. A straightforward approach using time-accurate simulation is computationally expensive. The gap-enumeration method is a more efficient approach for computing actual response time in the P-FRP execution model. However, the implementation of this algorithm is difficult due to the requirement of a self-balancing tree and a complex gap-transformation function We have presented the game-board method using both fixed and dynamic size time intervals. The game-board, presented in this paper can be implemented with an array and has a simple set of rules. However, this approach leads to some slack in performance due to higher search costs.

In future work, we will be extending this method to account for situations where the values t copy (k) and t restore (k) could be variable. Developing methods to reduce the time for idle-period search will also be undertaken. We also plan to apply this technique to determining exact response time in other transaction based execution models like in [11], [1].
